title: 2016 resignation as Air Force commander over NATO air policing, and Borisov's accusation that he 'lied'
description: Radev resigned as commander of the Bulgarian Air Force on 1 August 2016, formally citing the compulsory release age, shortly before the Bulgarian Socialist Party approached him as a possible presidential candidate. At a BTA news conference on 16 August he said he had 'never been against the joint guarding of Bulgaria's airspace with the country's allies', but objected to the concept for joint NATO air policing approved by Defence Minister Nikolai Nenchev in February 2016, under which Bulgaria would pay the costs of visiting allied air forces; he called it 'more degrading than the Treaty of Neuilly-sur-Seine' and blamed the ministry's leadership for the grounding of the MiG-29 fleet. Nenchev said Radev's only motive was disagreement with a law passed by parliament allowing foreign forces to help police Bulgarian airspace. Prime Minister Boyko Borisov said on 2 August that Radev had 'lied' to him about having no political ambitions; according to the Sofia Globe, Borisov had talked him out of an earlier resignation in October 2015.
key_facts: Resignation submitted 1 August 2016; released from military service in August 2016
Radev: the paid joint air-policing concept was 'unfavourable and degrading' for Bulgaria
Borisov: 'So he lied to me'; the BSP nominated Radev for President later in August

title: Statement that Crimea was 'currently Russian' (2021 presidential campaign)
description: In a televised debate with Anastas Gerdzhikov before the 21 November 2021 presidential run-off, Radev said that 'the sanctions that were imposed as a result of Crimea and Ukraine are not yielding results' and that Crimea was 'currently Russian' (Reuters, via Euronews). According to Reuters he had taken office in 2017 after a campaign that called for the lifting of sanctions against Russia. On 19 November Ukraine's Foreign Ministry summoned the Bulgarian ambassador and said it expected Radev to retract his comments; Radev's press office said he had repeatedly stated that the annexation of Crimea violated international law, that legally Crimea belongs to Ukraine, and that 'currently' it is controlled by Russia (Novinite). On 22 November the US Embassy in Sofia said the United States was 'deeply concerned' by the remarks. Radev won the run-off.
key_facts: 18 November 2021 debate: Crimea 'currently Russian'; call for pragmatic ties with Russia
19 November 2021: Ukraine summons Bulgaria's ambassador
22 November 2021: US Embassy 'deeply concerned'

title: 2020 prosecution searches in the Presidency and investigation of his legal adviser Plamen Uzunov
description: In 2020 the Prosecutor's Office under Prosecutor General Ivan Geshev investigated Plamen Uzunov, President Radev's secretary for legal affairs and anti-corruption, for trading in influence, over an SMS exchange with businessman Plamen Bobokov, who had been charged in an illegal waste-import case; prosecutors alleged that in December 2018 Uzunov had sent Bobokov an unsigned Supreme Administrative Court decision on the release of the ship BADR. On 2 July 2020 Radev called on the prosecution to release immediately the entire chat between him and Bobokov (BTA). On 9 July 2020 Uzunov was detained and his office in the Presidency was searched; the State Agency for National Security withdrew access to classified information from two senior officials of the presidential administration identified as P.U. and I.M. (BNT). In a televised address on 11 July 2020 Radev called on the Borisov government and the Prosecutor General to resign, as anti-corruption protests grew (Euronews). On 6 February 2023 the Sofia City Prosecution Office announced that it had closed the investigation against Uzunov and Bobokov (BTA). Radev was not a party to these proceedings and was not charged.
key_facts: 9 July 2020: Uzunov detained; Presidency office searched
11 July 2020: Radev demands the resignation of the government and the Prosecutor General
6 February 2023: investigation against Uzunov and Bobokov closed by the Sofia City Prosecution Office
Radev himself was not a suspect or defendant

title: Opposition to arms for Ukraine as President and clash with Zelenskyy (2022–2023)
description: As President, Radev opposed Bulgarian military support for Ukraine after Russia's full-scale invasion, saying it risked drawing Bulgaria into the war (OSW). During Volodymyr Zelenskyy's visit to Sofia on 6 July 2023, at the invitation of the Denkov government, Radev said in their meeting at the Presidency, broadcast live, that 'the provision of more and more weapons will hardly lead to' a solution; Zelenskyy asked him what he would do 'if you are not helped with weapons by people who share your values', and Radev soon afterwards asked the media to leave (Sofia Globe). Radev said he had 'always defended the Bulgarian interest and not the interest of other countries' (BTA). On 14 July 2023 he said Ukraine was 'insisting on waging this war', that 'the bill is being paid by the whole of Europe' and that the government should 'stop seeing the Bulgarian armed forces as a warehouse' of a foreign army; the Ukrainian embassy replied that blaming Ukraine was 'one of the most common supporting theses of Russian propaganda', and Prime Minister Nikolai Denkov said the Presidency was 'constantly issuing provocations'. On 4 December 2023 Radev vetoed the ratification of the donation of armoured personnel carriers to Ukraine; parliament overrode the veto.
key_facts: 6 July 2023: Zelenskyy–Radev meeting; press asked to leave
14–15 July 2023: Radev's statements and the Ukrainian embassy's rebuke
4 December 2023: veto of the APC donation to Ukraine, later overridden

title: Botas gas agreement signed under the caretaker government he appointed (2023) and its 2026 freeze
description: On 3 January 2023, under the caretaker government of Galab Donev appointed by President Radev, state gas supplier Bulgargaz signed an agreement with Türkiye's BOTAS booking 106.4 GWh a day of capacity at Turkish LNG terminals for about BGN 1 million a day until 2035, payable whether or not it is used; by May 2026 Bulgargaz's arrears were about BGN 300 million and BTA reports that rescinding the deal would expose it to close to BGN 3 billion in damages. The contract has been widely criticised as unfavourable to Bulgaria, and in April 2024 parliament instructed the energy minister to seek its renegotiation; Radev has defended it, saying previous governments did not use it properly (Sofia Globe). As Prime Minister he obtained on 6 July 2026 a 15-month suspension during which Bulgaria pays only for capacity used; Democratic Bulgaria MP Ivaylo Mirchev asked 'What has Bulgaria promised Turkiye to make this happen?'. Galab Donev, caretaker Prime Minister when the deal was signed, is Finance Minister in Radev's government.
key_facts: Signed 3 January 2023 under the Donev caretaker cabinet appointed by Radev
Take-or-pay: about BGN 1 million (EUR 512,000) a day until 2035
6 July 2026: 15-month freeze after Radev–Erdoğan talks; renegotiation pending
Radev: arrears of about USD 360 million, no payments since July 2024

title: 2025 proposal for a referendum on adopting the euro
description: On 9 May 2025, weeks before the convergence reports on Bulgaria's euro accession, President Radev proposed that the National Assembly call a national referendum on whether Bulgarians agreed to the introduction of the euro in 2026, arguing that it required broad public consent. National Assembly Chair Nataliya Kiselova rejected the proposal on 13 May as inadmissible under national and EU law. His legal secretary Krum Zarkov resigned, later telling BNT that he had advised Radev in writing that such a referendum would be unconstitutional (Novinite). On Radev's petition, the Constitutional Court ruled on 18 November 2025 that the Chair had no power to decide on the admissibility of a referendum proposal; Radev called it 'a victory of law over an arbitrary act of the political class'. Parliament then rejected the proposal on 3 December 2025 by 135 votes to 81, with three abstentions; the Presidency did not send a representative to the debate. Bulgaria joined the euro area on 1 January 2026.
key_facts: 9 May 2025: referendum proposal; 13 May: rejected by the Speaker
Legal secretary Krum Zarkov resigned over the proposal
18 November 2025: Constitutional Court rules the Speaker lacked competence
3 December 2025: parliament votes the proposal down, 135–81–3

title: Push to remove Patriarch Kirill and Lukoil founder Vagit Alekperov from EU sanctions (2026)
description: On 18 June 2026 Radev said Bulgaria would ask for Patriarch Kirill, head of the Russian Orthodox Church, who has publicly supported Russia's war against Ukraine, to be removed from the EU's next sanctions package (Kyiv Independent). He justified the objection by saying 'the time of crusades' was over, and said that sanctioning Vagit Alekperov, founder of Lukoil, would mean 'shooting ourselves in the foot'. In July Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova confirmed that both men, as well as a Russian citizen linked to spare parts for the Sofia metro, had been dropped from the proposed 21st package and that Bulgaria would support it; she said defending the national position 'does not lead to isolation' (Novinite).
key_facts: 18 June 2026: Radev announces Bulgaria will seek Kirill's removal
July 2026: Kirill and Alekperov removed from the draft 21st package at Bulgaria's request
Lukoil is sanctioned by the US and the UK; Alekperov by the UK, Australia, Canada and New Zealand (Novinite)

title: Ending military aid to Ukraine and European Parliament criticism of Sofia's response to Russian attacks in the Black Sea (2026)
description: The government's decision of 10 June 2026 to stop supplying weapons from army stocks to Ukraine drew criticism from the opposition: GERB's Georg Georgiev said it jeopardised Bulgaria's strategic posture and sent mixed signals to allies, and Democratic Bulgaria's Ivaylo Mirchev said the decisions were 'more likely to cater for Vladimir Putin's wishes' (BTA). On 21 October the cabinet invoked 'constructive abstention' on European Peace Facility funding for lethal weapons, saying Bulgaria supports Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity but 'rejects the logic of endless military confrontation'. After drone strikes on merchant ships off Bulgaria and Romania, including the Malta-flagged Chelsea-3 on 13 October 2026, the European Parliament adopted on 22 October a resolution (432–52–88) holding Russia responsible, regretting 'Sofia's weak diplomatic response to Russia' and calling on Radev to 'match demands for allied solidarity with concrete action' and to stop delaying Bulgaria's participation in a NATO anti-drone initiative.
key_facts: 10 June 2026: arms supplies from army stocks halted
21 October 2026: constructive abstention on EPF lethal aid
22 October 2026: European Parliament resolution criticises the Bulgarian government's response

title: 2026 budget: record deficit, new debt and partial annulment by the Constitutional Court
description: The 2026 State Budget Act, adopted on 24 July 2026 by 125 votes to 84, provides for a deficit of 5.7% of GDP and up to EUR 10.1 billion in new debt. Former GERB finance minister Temenuzhka Petkova called it a 'scandalous' budget; Continue the Change asked President Iliana Iotova to veto it, which she declined to do. Finance Minister Galab Donev said the budget brought accumulated liabilities to light and that the deficit was inherited. The budget package also froze the minimum wage at EUR 620.20 and closed the commission on the State Security files, transferring its functions to the Archives State Agency. On referrals by MPs and the Ombudsman, the Constitutional Court ruled on 20 October 2026 that the minimum-wage freeze, the change in the calculation of length of service and a new pay formula for junior magistrates were unconstitutional, while rejecting the request to annul the whole Act.
key_facts: Deficit 5.7% of GDP; borrowing ceiling EUR 10.1 billion
29 July 2026: President Iotova rejects calls to veto the budget
20 October 2026: Constitutional Court strikes down the minimum-wage freeze and two other provisions

title: Detention of a local activist during his visit to flood-hit Strumyani (August 2026)
description: During Radev's visit to the flood-hit village of Strumyani on 28 August 2026, a local activist was handcuffed and taken to a police station for identification; a video of the arrest prompted demands for explanations from Yes, Bulgaria co-chair Ivaylo Mirchev and the Association of European Journalists – Bulgaria, and the opposition accused the National Service for Protection (NSP) and the police of isolating residents and the press from the Prime Minister. The NSP said it had neither been instructed to restrict nor had restricted access, and that the person had refused to show an ID or press card; the government press office said footage showed people, including the activist, had free access to Radev and that the circumstances were being investigated, as Radev had also called for. Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev removed the head of the Blagoevgrad police, saying the officers' response 'exceeded what was necessary'.
key_facts: 28 August 2026: activist detained during the Prime Minister's visit
Blagoevgrad regional police director dismissed
NSP and government press office deny restricting access to the Prime Minister
